title: Intro to AI
description: Learn GRE words through agents, search, logic, knowledge representation, planning, reasoning under uncertainty and machine learning.

cards.sentence: ELIZA, a 1966 pattern-matching chatbot, convinced some gullible users that it understood them.
cards.explanation: Weizenbaum's ELIZA turned user statements into questions with scripted rules, and its DOCTOR script imitated a psychotherapist. The Turing test, proposed in 1950 as the 'imitation game', has the same weakness: judges can be fooled by surface fluency without real understanding.

cards.sentence: The 1955 proposal for the Dartmouth workshop made the audacious claim that every feature of intelligence could be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it.
cards.explanation: Proposed by McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon, the 1956 summer workshop is where the term 'artificial intelligence' was coined, and it is usually treated as the field's founding event.

cards.sentence: Cuts in funding after unmet promises pushed AI into a torpor in the 1970s and again in the late 1980s, periods known as AI winters.
cards.explanation: The first followed critiques such as the 1973 Lighthill report in the UK, and the second followed the collapse of the market for expert-system hardware and software. Interest recovered with machine learning, more data and faster computers.

cards.sentence: A fledgling learning agent starts with little knowledge and improves through experience.
cards.explanation: Russell and Norvig describe a learning agent with four parts: a performance element that selects actions, a learning element that improves it, a critic that gives feedback, and a problem generator that suggests exploratory actions.

citations.title: Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (Russell & Norvig)

cards.sentence: Perfect rationality is a paragon that real agents cannot reach, because they have limited time and computation.
cards.explanation: A rational agent chooses the action expected to maximize its performance measure given what it has perceived. Bounded rationality, a term from Herbert Simon, accepts good-enough decisions made within resource limits.

cards.sentence: Expert systems tried to capture the rules of a human sage, such as an experienced physician, in an if-then knowledge base.
cards.explanation: MYCIN, built in the 1970s, used several hundred rules to recommend antibiotics for bacterial infections and could explain its reasoning. Building and maintaining such rule bases was costly, a problem called the knowledge acquisition bottleneck.

cards.sentence: Breadth-first search is assiduous, expanding every node at depth d before any node at depth d + 1.
cards.explanation: It finds the shallowest goal, so it is optimal when every step costs the same, but its memory use grows as b^d for branching factor b. Uniform-cost search generalizes it to steps with different costs.

cards.sentence: In greedy best-first search, the heuristic goads the search toward nodes that look closest to the goal.
cards.explanation: Greedy search expands the node with the lowest estimated distance h(n) to the goal. It is fast but neither complete nor optimal in general. A* uses f(n) = g(n) + h(n) to balance the cost so far against the estimated cost remaining.

cards.sentence: A heuristic that gouges by overestimating the true remaining cost is inadmissible and can make A* return a suboptimal path.
cards.explanation: An admissible heuristic never overestimates, which makes A* tree search optimal. A consistent heuristic satisfies h(n) ≤ c(n, n′) + h(n′), which keeps A* graph search optimal without re-expanding nodes.

cards.sentence: Hill climbing can vacillate on a plateau, moving between equal-valued states without making progress.
cards.explanation: Local search keeps only a current state and moves to a better neighbor. It can stall at local maxima and plateaus, so variants add random restarts, limits on sideways moves, tabu lists, or simulated annealing, which sometimes accepts worse moves with a probability that falls over time.

cards.sentence: Minimax assumes an implacable opponent who always plays the move that is best for them.
cards.explanation: In a two-player zero-sum game, MAX picks the move that maximizes the worst-case outcome, assuming MIN plays optimally. That is optimal against a perfect opponent but can be too cautious against a weaker one.

cards.sentence: Alpha-beta pruning can dismiss whole branches of the game tree once they cannot change the final decision.
cards.explanation: It returns the same move as plain minimax. With good move ordering it examines about b^(m/2) nodes instead of b^m, which roughly doubles the depth that can be searched in the same time.

cards.sentence: Chess programs keep searching past the nominal depth until the position is quiescent, so they do not judge a position in the middle of a capture sequence.
cards.explanation: This is quiescence search. It reduces the horizon effect, in which a fixed-depth search misses a looming loss just beyond its cutoff, by evaluating only positions with no pending captures or checks.

cards.sentence: Shannon estimated chess at about 10¹²⁰ possible games, a number that would daunt any exhaustive search.
cards.explanation: Real programs rely on heuristic evaluation, pruning and depth limits. Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in a 1997 match using specialized hardware that searched on the order of 200 million positions per second.

cards.definition: without deceit; by extension, never leading to false conclusions
cards.sentence: A sound inference procedure is guileless: from true premises it never derives a false conclusion.
cards.explanation: Soundness means everything derived is entailed by the knowledge base, and completeness means everything entailed can be derived. Resolution refutation is both sound and refutation-complete for first-order logic.

cards.sentence: Unification is conciliatory: it finds a substitution that makes two logical expressions identical.
cards.explanation: For example, unifying Knows(John, x) with Knows(y, Mary) gives the substitution {y/John, x/Mary}. Unification is the key step in first-order resolution and in the backward chaining used by Prolog.

cards.sentence: A knowledge base containing discordant facts is inconsistent, and in classical logic anything follows from a contradiction.
cards.explanation: This is the principle of explosion. Practical systems therefore check consistency, use reason-maintenance systems to retract beliefs, or use probabilistic or paraconsistent methods that tolerate conflicts.

cards.sentence: Concluding that every bird flies from a few observed birds is a precipitate inference: plausible, but not guaranteed.
cards.explanation: Deduction preserves truth, while induction generalizes from examples and can be wrong. Penguins and ostriches are counterexamples, which is why inductive conclusions carry uncertainty.

cards.sentence: Default rules such as 'birds fly' are qualified by exceptions like penguins, so reasoning with them must be able to retract conclusions.
cards.explanation: Classical logic is monotonic: adding facts never removes conclusions. Default logic and other nonmonotonic formalisms let an agent conclude that Tweety flies until it learns that Tweety is a penguin.

cards.sentence: The closed-world assumption is presumptuous: anything not known to be true is treated as false.
cards.explanation: Databases and Prolog use negation as failure, which is efficient but wrong when the knowledge is incomplete. The open-world assumption, used in OWL and the semantic web, treats unknown facts as unknown.

cards.sentence: The frame problem asks how to say that most facts remain inert after an action without listing them all.
cards.explanation: Moving a block does not change its color or the weather. Situation calculus needed frame axioms for every unchanged fact. Successor-state axioms address this, and so do planning languages such as STRIPS, which assume anything not mentioned is unchanged.

cards.definition: disclaim or disavow; retract a previous statement; openly confess error
cards.sentence: When a partial assignment leads to a dead end, a backtracking CSP solver must recant its last choice and try another value.
cards.explanation: A constraint satisfaction problem has variables, domains and constraints. Backtracking search assigns one variable at a time, and heuristics such as minimum remaining values, forward checking and arc consistency (AC-3) prune the search.

cards.definition: plan of a trip; by extension, a planned sequence of steps
cards.sentence: A plan is an itinerary of actions that leads from the initial state to the goal.
cards.explanation: In STRIPS-style planning each action has preconditions and effects, and the planner searches for a sequence whose effects achieve the goal. PDDL is the standard language for describing planning problems.

cards.sentence: Partial-order planners are deliberately indolent about ordering: they leave steps unordered until a conflict forces a decision.
cards.explanation: This least-commitment strategy avoids early arbitrary choices and backtracking. The plan keeps causal links and ordering constraints, and threats to a link are resolved by adding orderings.

cards.definition: doubter; person who suspends judgment until having examined evidence supporting a point of view
cards.sentence: A Bayesian agent behaves like a skeptic who updates its beliefs in proportion to the strength of the evidence.
cards.explanation: Bayes' rule gives P(H | e) = P(e | H) P(H) / P(e). A rare disease stays unlikely even after a positive test that has false positives, which is why base rates matter.

cards.sentence: Naive Bayes rests on an ingenuous assumption that features are independent given the class, yet it often classifies well.
cards.explanation: The assumption turns P(features | class) into a simple product, so training and prediction are cheap. The probabilities can be poorly calibrated when features are strongly correlated, but the ranking of classes is often still right.

cards.definition: impervious; not permitting passage through its substance
cards.sentence: In a Bayesian network, observing the middle node of a chain can make the path impermeable, so its two ends become independent.
cards.explanation: This is d-separation. In A → B → C, knowing B blocks influence between A and C. In a collider A → B ← C, observing B or one of its descendants makes A and C dependent, an effect called explaining away.

cards.sentence: A risk-averse agent has a penchant for sure things, which a concave utility function captures.
cards.explanation: Expected-utility theory says to choose the action with the highest expected utility. With concave utility, a guaranteed $50 can be preferred to a coin flip for $100 or nothing, even though both have the same expected value.

cards.sentence: In the Bellman equation, a state's value is derivative: it is computed from the values of its successor states.
cards.explanation: In a Markov decision process, V(s) = max over a of the sum over s′ of P(s′ | s, a) [R(s, a, s′) + γV(s′)]. Value iteration applies this update repeatedly until the values converge, and the greedy policy for the converged values is optimal.

cards.sentence: In a POMDP, walls or poor sensors can occlude the agent's view, so it must keep a belief state over where it might be.
cards.explanation: A partially observable MDP replaces the known state with a probability distribution over states, updated after each action and observation. Solving POMDPs exactly is computationally very hard, so approximate methods are used.

cards.sentence: A purely random policy is desultory: it explores widely but never uses what it has learned.
cards.explanation: Epsilon-greedy balances exploration and exploitation by choosing a random action with probability ε and the best-known action otherwise. The value of ε is often decayed over time.

cards.sentence: An agent that is dogmatic about exploiting its current best action may never discover a better one.
cards.explanation: In a multi-armed bandit, always pulling the apparently best arm can lock in an early lucky estimate. Methods such as UCB and Thompson sampling explore in proportion to their uncertainty.

cards.sentence: In reinforcement learning, a negative reward acts as castigation, discouraging the actions that led to it.
cards.explanation: Q-learning updates Q(s, a) toward r + γ max Q(s′, a′), so negative rewards lower the value of actions that lead to bad outcomes. A badly designed reward can be exploited, with the agent maximizing it in unintended ways.

cards.sentence: An unpruned decision tree can distend until every leaf holds a single training example, which memorizes noise.
cards.explanation: Tree learners choose splits that maximize information gain or reduce Gini impurity. Limiting depth, requiring a minimum leaf size, or pruning on validation data reduces overfitting.

cards.definition: hard to understand; known only to the chosen few
cards.sentence: The learned weights of a deep network are esoteric: even its designers cannot easily read off why a particular decision was made.
cards.explanation: Explainable AI methods such as LIME and SHAP approximate which input features drove a prediction. Their explanations are themselves approximations, so they should be validated before being trusted.

citations.title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions (SHAP) (arXiv)

cards.sentence: A beneficent AI system should pursue goals that actually match human values, which is the value alignment problem.
cards.explanation: Specifying objectives exactly is hard, and an agent that optimizes a flawed proxy, such as a poorly written reward function, can find loopholes. Approaches include learning from human feedback and inverse reinforcement learning to infer what people want.

citations.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences (arXiv)
